articleText.footer: General information, not a diagnosis. A qualified clinician can help with symptoms that concern you. This app is not an emergency service.

perimenopause-and-hormones.title: Perimenopause and hormones
perimenopause-and-hormones.teaser: Understand the change without making assumptions.

body.0: Perimenopause is the transition towards menopause, when hormone levels change and periods may become less predictable. Natural menopause is usually identified after 12 months without a period, when there is no other cause.
body.1: Experiences differ: some women have few symptoms; others find daily life harder. Her experience deserves to be heard, rather than compared with someone else’s.

perimenopause-and-hormones.partnerAction: Ask what she has noticed and what she wants you to understand. Let her decide how much to share.
perimenopause-and-hormones.teenAction: You can learn about this stage without asking Mum for private details. You did not cause these changes.
perimenopause-and-hormones.saying: I may not understand everything yet, but I want to learn.

sleep-and-restless-nights.title: Sleep and restless nights
sleep-and-restless-nights.teaser: Being in bed does not always mean getting rest.

body.0: Difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep can happen during this transition. A long night in bed may still include many interruptions. The next morning, patience and concentration can feel harder to find.
body.1: Protecting rest is a practical way to show care, while ongoing sleep difficulties deserve professional attention.

sleep-and-restless-nights.partnerAction: Agree on a comfortable bedroom temperature and take responsibility for one morning task after a difficult night.
sleep-and-restless-nights.teenAction: Keep late-night noise low and organise your school or college things yourself.
sleep-and-restless-nights.saying: Would a quieter evening or help with the morning routine make things easier?

low-energy-and-fatigue.title: Low energy and fatigue
low-energy-and-fatigue.teaser: Tiredness is not a measure of effort.

body.0: Fatigue can be linked to poor sleep, stress or hormonal changes, but other causes include anaemia, thyroid problems and sleep apnoea. Avoid deciding that it is “just menopause” or laziness.
body.1: If tiredness persists for weeks or affects everyday life, encourage a medical appointment. She should not have to prove she is exhausted before getting help.

low-energy-and-fatigue.partnerAction: Take over a complete task, such as planning and preparing dinner, rather than waiting for detailed instructions.
low-energy-and-fatigue.teenAction: Choose one manageable responsibility, such as clearing your dishes, without giving up your own rest or studies.
low-energy-and-fatigue.saying: I can take care of dinner tonight. You don’t need to supervise.

brain-fog-and-forgetfulness.title: Brain fog and forgetfulness
brain-fog-and-forgetfulness.teaser: A forgotten word does not erase her ability.

body.0: Some women notice difficulty concentrating or remembering things during perimenopause, and poor sleep may make this worse. Give her time to finish a thought instead of testing her memory, teasing her or taking over.
body.1: If changes persist, worsen or interfere with daily life, support a medical review. Sudden confusion or new speech difficulty needs urgent medical help; it should not be labelled brain fog.

brain-fog-and-forgetfulness.partnerAction: Offer a shared calendar or written reminder only if she finds it useful.
brain-fog-and-forgetfulness.teenAction: Give one piece of information at a time and repeat it kindly if asked.
brain-fog-and-forgetfulness.saying: Take your time. Would you like me to write that down?

mood-changes-and-emotions.title: Mood changes and emotions
mood-changes-and-emotions.teaser: Listen to the feeling, not just the tone.

body.0: Mood changes can happen during perimenopause, and tiredness may make emotions harder to manage. That does not mean every concern is caused by hormones.
body.1: A complaint about feeling unsupported may point to a real problem that needs attention. Listen to what is being said. Everyone in the family still deserves respectful treatment.

mood-changes-and-emotions.partnerAction: Ask about the concern itself before offering an explanation. Acknowledge your part if something needs to change.
mood-changes-and-emotions.teenAction: You are allowed to say a conversation feels hurtful and take a break. You are not responsible for fixing Mum’s mood.
mood-changes-and-emotions.saying: I hear that you’re upset. What would you like me to understand?

hot-flashes-and-night-sweats.title: Hot flashes and night sweats
hot-flashes-and-night-sweats.teaser: A little practical comfort can mean a lot.

body.0: A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat that may come with sweating. When this happens at night, it can interrupt sleep.
body.1: Ask what feels comfortable: a fan, a cooler room or a drink may help. Do not make jokes, announce it to others or insist she must feel the same temperature as you.

hot-flashes-and-night-sweats.partnerAction: Keep an extra sheet or towel available if she wants one, and agree on bedding that works for both of you.
hot-flashes-and-night-sweats.teenAction: Offer water or help adjust the fan, then let Mum decide whether she wants company.
hot-flashes-and-night-sweats.saying: Would you like the fan on, some water, or a little space?

stress-worry-and-anxiety.title: Stress, worry and anxiety
stress-worry-and-anxiety.teaser: A calm response starts with taking her seriously.

body.0: Anxiety can occur around menopause, but work, relationships and other health concerns may also contribute. Saying “stop overthinking” rarely opens a helpful conversation.
body.1: Ask what feels difficult and avoid adding pressure to explain everything immediately. When worry is persistent or disrupts ordinary activities, encourage professional support rather than expecting the family to manage it alone.

stress-worry-and-anxiety.partnerAction: Offer to sit with her or help with one specific source of pressure. Ask before suggesting a relaxation exercise.
stress-worry-and-anxiety.teenAction: You can be kind without becoming Mum’s counsellor. Tell a trusted adult if you feel worried or overwhelmed.
stress-worry-and-anxiety.saying: Would you like company, a quieter space, or help finding support?

joint-pain-and-stiffness.title: Joint pain and stiffness
joint-pain-and-stiffness.teaser: Pain deserves care, even when it is invisible.

body.0: Joint aches may occur during perimenopause, but injury and conditions such as arthritis can also cause pain. Avoid assuming all stiffness is hormonal.
body.1: Pain that keeps returning, affects sleep or limits activity deserves medical advice. A hot, swollen joint, especially with fever or feeling unwell, needs urgent assessment.

joint-pain-and-stiffness.partnerAction: Offer help with a task that hurts and support movement at her comfortable pace, without pushing through pain.
joint-pain-and-stiffness.teenAction: Carry a manageable bag or help with a small chore if asked. Leave medicines and treatment decisions to adults and clinicians.
joint-pain-and-stiffness.saying: Which part of today feels physically difficult? I can help with that.

changing-periods.title: Changing periods
changing-periods.teaser: Understand the change while respecting privacy.

body.0: Periods can become less predictable during perimenopause. Bleeding that is unusually heavy, lasts longer than expected or occurs between periods needs medical discussion. Bleeding after menopause needs checking even if it happens only once.
body.1: Support should make things easier, not turn her cycle into a family conversation she has not agreed to.

changing-periods.partnerAction: Offer to buy her preferred period products or help arrange an appointment if she wants. Do not ask for access to her cycle logs.
changing-periods.teenAction: Treat period products as ordinary essentials. Avoid jokes about leaks, stains or bathroom breaks.
changing-periods.saying: Would you like me to pick anything up or help with something practical?

body-changes-and-confidence.title: Body changes and confidence
body-changes-and-confidence.teaser: She deserves comfort without comments on her size.

body.0: Body shape may change around menopause. Whether or not she talks about it, avoid making weight, food or appearance the centre of family attention. Uninvited diet advice can feel like criticism.
body.1: Ask what helps her feel comfortable and confident, and remember to notice her humour, skills and interests too.

body-changes-and-confidence.partnerAction: Invite her to an activity you can enjoy together without presenting it as a weight-loss project. Respect a no.
body-changes-and-confidence.teenAction: Avoid jokes about Mum’s body or comparing her with older photos. Compliment something you appreciate about her as a person.
body-changes-and-confidence.saying: I love spending time with you. What would feel good to do together?

listen-before-trying-to-solve.title: Listen before trying to solve
listen-before-trying-to-solve.teaser: Sometimes being heard is the help she wants.

body.0: When someone shares a difficult day, advice can arrive before understanding. Start by letting her finish. Reflect back what you heard, then ask what kind of response she wants.
body.1: Listening does not require agreeing with everything or knowing the perfect answer. It means making room for her experience without immediately correcting it.

listen-before-trying-to-solve.partnerAction: Put your phone aside and ask permission before giving advice or suggesting a solution.
listen-before-trying-to-solve.teenAction: You can listen for a short time and still say when you need to return to homework or rest.
listen-before-trying-to-solve.saying: Would you like me to listen, help with something, or give you some space?

share-the-mental-load.title: Share the mental load
share-the-mental-load.teaser: Remembering the task is part of doing it.

body.0: Household work includes noticing what is needed, planning it and following through. If she must remind everyone repeatedly, she is still managing the task.
body.1: Agree on responsibilities that each person can own from start to finish. Sharing the load should be an ordinary family habit, not something she has to earn by having a difficult day.

share-the-mental-load.partnerAction: Own a recurring task, including planning and follow-up, such as grocery shopping or arranging a repair.
share-the-mental-load.teenAction: Take charge of an age-appropriate task, such as your school bag or putting away your laundry. You do not need to run the household.
share-the-mental-load.saying: I’ll handle this from start to finish. You don’t need to remind me.

give-space-and-stay-connected.title: Give space and stay connected
give-space-and-stay-connected.teaser: A quiet moment can coexist with closeness.

body.0: Wanting time alone does not automatically mean someone is angry or rejecting you. Ask what she needs instead of guessing.
body.1: A short pause can be easier when everyone knows whether and when to reconnect. Space should be a choice, not a punishment or a reason to ignore each other indefinitely.

give-space-and-stay-connected.partnerAction: Ask whether she would like company or privacy, then agree on a suitable time to check in if she wants that.
give-space-and-stay-connected.teenAction: Let Mum know you are available, then continue your own activities. You do not need to keep checking whether she is okay.
give-space-and-stay-connected.saying: Would you prefer some quiet time? Shall we catch up after dinner?

handle-disagreements-with-care.title: Handle disagreements with care

body.0: Disagreements still need to be addressed. Avoid “you’re hormonal” or “you always overreact”; these phrases dismiss the issue. Talk about one specific event and what each person needs next.
body.1: If the conversation becomes heated, pause and return when it feels safe and calmer. Symptoms never excuse threats, humiliation or violence.

handle-disagreements-with-care.partnerAction: Acknowledge your own behaviour and agree on one practical change rather than trying to win the argument.
handle-disagreements-with-care.teenAction: You do not have to mediate adult disagreements. Step away if you feel unsafe and contact a trusted adult or emergency help if there is danger.
handle-disagreements-with-care.saying: I want to work this out, but let’s pause until we can speak respectfully.

supporting-mum-while-being-a-teen.title: Supporting Mum while being a teen
supporting-mum-while-being-a-teen.teaser: You can care without carrying everything.

body.0: If Mum seems tired, distracted or different, it is okay to have questions. You did not cause her symptoms and you are not responsible for making them disappear.
body.1: Small acts of kindness can help, but your schoolwork, friendships, sleep and feelings matter too. You should not be expected to manage medicines, monitor symptoms or keep adult worries secret.

supporting-mum-while-being-a-teen.teenAction: Choose one small, manageable way to help. If things feel too heavy, talk to another parent, a relative, a teacher or a school counsellor. Ask for help immediately if you feel unsafe.
supporting-mum-while-being-a-teen.saying: I care about you, Mum. I can help with this, but I need time for myself too.

privacy-consent-and-trust.title: Privacy, consent and trust
privacy-consent-and-trust.teaser: Being family does not mean access to everything.

body.0: Supporting someone does not give you automatic access to their health information. She decides what to share, with whom and when.
body.1: A quiet day or an unanswered question is not permission to check her phone or tracker. Respecting privacy helps make family support feel safe.

privacy-consent-and-trust.partnerAction: Ask before discussing her symptoms with relatives or clinicians, or forwarding a report. Accept it if she changes her mind about sharing.
privacy-consent-and-trust.teenAction: You do not need to read Mum’s health logs to be supportive. Learn from general articles and ask respectful questions.
privacy-consent-and-trust.saying: Share only what feels comfortable. I won’t pass it on without asking.

when-professional-help-is-needed.title: When professional help is needed
when-professional-help-is-needed.teaser: Family support and clinical care can work together.

body.0: Encourage a medical appointment when symptoms are new, worsening, persistent or disrupting daily life. Do not wait for every period to stop before seeking advice.
body.1: Ask whether she wants help arranging the visit, and let her speak for herself.
body.2: In an emergency, including sudden speech difficulty, one-sided weakness or immediate risk of self-harm, call 112 in India. Do not wait for an app reply.

when-professional-help-is-needed.partnerAction: Offer practical appointment support without choosing treatments for her or insisting on being present.
when-professional-help-is-needed.teenAction: Tell a trusted adult if you are worried. In immediate danger, contact emergency help; you do not need to handle the situation alone.
when-professional-help-is-needed.saying: Would you like help arranging an appointment, or would you prefer to do that privately?

closeness-and-intimacy.title: Closeness and intimacy
closeness-and-intimacy.teaser: Connection begins with comfort and consent.

body.0: Vaginal dryness can make sex uncomfortable, and changes in desire may occur around menopause. Do not assume discomfort or a no means a lack of love.
body.1: Ask what kind of closeness feels welcome, with no expectation that affection must lead to sex. Stop if there is pain. Persistent discomfort or bleeding after sex needs medical advice; treatment options are available.

closeness-and-intimacy.partnerAction: Have a private conversation outside an intimate moment. Let her choose whether she wants to explore clinical support. Shared chores or gifts never create an obligation to be intimate.
closeness-and-intimacy.saying: There’s no pressure. What kind of closeness feels comfortable for you?

sleep.headline: Send her a thoughtful message
sleep.body: A small gesture may help after a difficult night’s sleep. Try to take something off her plate today.

mood.headline: Ask, then listen
mood.body: Mood shifts are hormonal, not personal. Asking how she is doing, and not trying to fix it, helps more than advice.

stress.headline: Take something off her list
stress.body: A stressful week eases fastest when the practical load lightens. Pick one thing and quietly handle it.

energy.headline: Keep today gentle
energy.body: Low energy is a symptom, not reluctance. A slower plan and an early night will do more than encouragement.

supportSteady.headline: A good week to say so
supportSteady.body: Nothing looks difficult right now. Noticing the steady weeks out loud is its own kind of support.

supportUnknown.headline: Let her know you are here
supportUnknown.body: There is nothing to read yet. A short message saying you are around is a good place to start.

sleep.headline: Poor sleep can affect energy and patience
sleep.body: Falling oestrogen interrupts sleep and raises night-time body temperature. The following day is harder for reasons that have nothing to do with willpower.

mood.headline: Mood changes are not always personal
mood.body: Hormonal fluctuation affects emotional regulation directly. A sharp reaction is usually the hormone, not the relationship.

stress.headline: Stress lands harder during perimenopause
stress.body: The same pressures feel heavier when hormones are shifting, because the body’s buffer against them is thinner than it used to be.

energy.headline: Fatigue here is physical
energy.body: Broken sleep, hot flushes and hormonal change together produce a tiredness that rest alone does not fully clear.

educationGeneral.headline: Perimenopause is a physical transition
educationGeneral.body: It can last years and affects sleep, mood, energy and memory. Knowing that helps everyone in the house take it less personally.

actionPendingReminder.title: Still on your list?
actionPendingReminder.body: A small gesture can still make today better.

0.headline: Mood changes aren’t always personal
0.body: Hormonal fluctuations can affect emotional regulation. Try not to read a difficult moment as a verdict on you.

1.headline: Sleep is the first thing to go
1.body: Night waking and heat episodes often arrive before anything else. Most of the hard days start the night before.

2.headline: Brain fog is real and temporary
2.body: Losing a word mid-sentence is a known symptom, not a sign of decline. Filling the gap for her is kinder than pointing it out.

3.headline: This is not a short phase
3.body: Perimenopause commonly runs four to eight years. Pacing your support matters more than an intense first month.

0.headline: Listen before trying to solve
0.body: Ask: “Would you like me to listen, help, or give you space?” It works because it hands the choice back to her.

1.headline: Offer specifics, not availability
1.body: “I’ll do dinner tonight” lands better than “let me know if you need anything”, which quietly makes it her job to ask.

2.headline: Keep the house cooler than you would choose
2.body: Heat episodes are worse in a warm room. It is a small concession with an outsized effect on her sleep.

3.headline: Do not diagnose out loud
3.body: Attributing every difficult moment to hormones is its own kind of dismissal. Believe the feeling first.

partner-general-01.text: She may not ask for support today. Give it anyway. ❤️

partner-general-02.text: Sometimes “I’m here” is all she needs to hear.

partner-stress-01.text: Her day looks heavy. Take one thing off her plate today.

partner-mood-01.text: A little patience today could mean a lot to her.

partner-sleep-01.text: She didn’t sleep well. A gentler morning might help.

partner-fatigue-01.text: She’s running low today. Help her slow down.

partner-hotflashes-01.text: She may be feeling uncomfortable. Keep things cool—and judgment-free.

partner-emotional-01.text: Don’t fix it. Just sit beside her and listen.

partner-connection-01.text: When did you last ask, “How are you really feeling?”

partner-appreciation-01.text: Tell her one thing you appreciate about her today.

partner-action-01.text: Tea. Hug. Quiet time. Your move. ❤️

partner-action-02.text: Surprise her with something small today. No occasion needed.

partner-action-03.text: Take over one chore before she asks.

partner-affection-01.text: One long hug can say more than ten questions.

partner-relationship-01.text: She’s changing. Your relationship can grow with her.

teen-general-01.text: Mum might be having a tough day. Be a little extra kind. ❤️

teen-general-02.text: One “How was your day, Mum?” can mean more than you think.

teen-fatigue-01.text: Mum looks tired? Help without waiting to be asked.

teen-mood-01.text: If Mum seems quiet today, give her a little space—and a little love.

teen-appreciation-01.text: Tell Mum something you love about her today.

teen-action-01.text: Tiny mission: make Mum smile once today. 😊

teen-action-02.text: Do one household job before Mum notices it needs doing.

teen-connection-01.text: Put the phone down for 10 minutes. Sit with Mum.

teen-emotional-01.text: Sometimes Mum needs understanding, not questions.

teen-gratitude-01.text: Send Mum a random “Love you.” No reason required.

teen-care-01.text: Ask Mum if she wants tea, water, or just company.

teen-awareness-01.text: Her body may be changing. Your kindness shouldn’t.

adult-general-01.text: Check in on her today—not just her symptoms.

adult-stress-01.text: She may be carrying more than she’s saying. Reach out.

adult-fatigue-01.text: Today might be a low-energy day. Help make things easier.

adult-connection-01.text: A two-minute call could completely change her day.

adult-support-01.text: Ask what she needs today instead of assuming.

adult-action-01.text: Small gesture. Big impact. Do something thoughtful today.

adult-appreciation-01.text: Remind her she’s valued beyond everything she does for others.

adult-isolation-01.text: Don’t let her go through a difficult day alone.

adult-selfcare-01.text: Encourage her to take some time for herself—then help make it possible.

impact-care-01.text: She takes care of everyone. Today, take care of her.

impact-emotional-01.text: You may not understand exactly what she’s feeling. You can still stand beside her.

impact-isolation-01.text: She doesn’t need you to have all the answers. She needs to know she isn’t alone.

impact-awareness-01.text: Perimenopause happens to her body. But how the family responds can change her experience.

impact-awareness-02.text: Don’t wait for her to say she’s struggling. Notice her.

impact-action-01.text: The most powerful support can sometimes be: “I’ve got this. You rest.”

suggestion.sleep: Start winding down half an hour earlier tonight. Screens down, lights low.
suggestion.energy: A short walk after lunch tends to do more for energy than another coffee.

hot_flash.2: This wave will crest and fade. You're handling it beautifully.
hot_flash.3: A cool cloth on your wrists or neck can take the edge off.
hot_flash.4: Nothing's wrong with you. This is your body adjusting, and it eases soon.

hot_flash.6: You're not alone in this. So many move through the same wave.
hot_flash.7: Find some air, drop your shoulders, and let it pass on its own time.
hot_flash.8: Each one you ride through, you understand your body a little more.
hot_flash.9: Be gentle with yourself right now. The flush will fade.

anxiety.1: Anxiety lies about how long it'll last. It always passes.
anxiety.2: Place a hand on your chest and feel it rise and fall. You're okay.
anxiety.3: Name five things you can see right now; let it pull you to the present.
anxiety.4: You don't have to fix anything this second. Just keep breathing.
anxiety.5: This feeling is a wave, not your whole ocean. It will recede.
anxiety.6: Be kind to yourself. You're carrying a lot and still showing up.
anxiety.7: Unclench your jaw, soften your hands. Your body can let go a little.
anxiety.8: You've moved through anxious moments before, and you will again.
anxiety.9: Slow your breath and the rest of you will follow. You're doing fine.

chills.1: A warm drink and a soft blanket can help settle the shivers.
chills.2: This is your body regulating. It'll pass. Stay cozy.

chills.4: Nothing to fight here. Bundle up and give yourself a moment.
chills.5: Your body's just balancing out. Warmth and rest will help.

chills.8: A warm shower or tea can coax the shivers away.

irritability.1: Step away for a breath if you can. The sharp edge softens with space.
irritability.2: You're allowed to feel irritable. Be as kind to yourself as you'd be to a friend.
irritability.3: This isn't the real you slipping. It's a passing surge. Go easy.
irritability.4: A short walk or a few deep breaths can loosen the tension.
irritability.5: Name what you need right now: quiet, space, water, a pause. Then take it.
irritability.6: Snapping doesn't make you a bad person. You're human and stretched thin.
irritability.7: Drop your shoulders, unclench your hands. Let some of it go.

irritability.9: Give yourself grace. You're managing more than anyone sees.

A.label: Vasomotor Module
A.dominantDomain: Hot flashes, night sweats, flushing, heart palpitations
A.trackerFocus: Log hot flash frequency, duration, and time of day. Note triggers: food, stress, temperature, alcohol.
A.introTail: Your most significant symptoms are vasomotor in nature. Hot flashes, night sweats, and related episodes are common in perimenopause and directly linked to fluctuating oestrogen. The good news: this domain responds well to both lifestyle and clinical interventions.

bullets.0: Keep sleep environment cool: 18–19°C is the evidence-backed optimal range
bullets.1: Wear layered, breathable cotton or bamboo fabrics; dress for easy temperature adjustment
bullets.2: Carry a small handheld fan for daytime episodes; cold water at onset (sip, don't gulp)
bullets.3: A cold pack on the back of the neck can abort or shorten a flash episode

bullets.0: Identify and reduce personal triggers: spicy food, alcohol if you use it, caffeine, and hot drinks are the most common
bullets.1: Regular moderate exercise reduces hot flash frequency within 8–12 weeks of consistent practice
bullets.2: Stress management is non-negotiable. Cortisol amplifies vasomotor symptoms significantly
bullets.3: Maintain a healthy weight; adipose tissue produces oestrone, and body weight affects symptom severity

2.title: Clinical options to discuss with your doctor

bullets.0: If symptoms are moderate to severe and disrupting daily life, ask your doctor about HRT eligibility
bullets.1: Non-hormonal options: low-dose SSRIs, SNRIs (venlafaxine), or gabapentin have evidence for vasomotor relief
bullets.2: Phytoestrogens (soy isoflavones, red clover): evidence is moderate; worth discussing with your doctor
bullets.3: Stellate ganglion block: an emerging clinical option for severe, treatment-resistant hot flashes

A.anuNote: ANU will prompt you to log hot flash episodes in real time. After 14 days, your pattern report will show peak times, average duration, and likely triggers. Many women are surprised to discover their triggers: the data often reveals what memory misses.

B.label: Psychological Module
B.dominantDomain: Irritability, mood swings, anxiety, depression, brain fog, memory difficulties
B.trackerFocus: Log mood (1–10), anxiety episodes, brain fog days, and sleep quality every evening.
B.introTail: Your most significant symptoms are in the psychological and cognitive domain. Mood changes, anxiety, and brain fog during perimenopause are neurological, driven by oestrogen's direct effect on serotonin, dopamine, and brain chemistry. This is not 'just stress.' It is real, it is hormonal, and it is addressable.

bullets.0: Identify mood triggers: hormonal dips often follow cycle patterns even when cycles are irregular
bullets.1: Mindfulness and breathwork: just 10 minutes daily has measurable, peer-reviewed effect on perimenopausal anxiety
bullets.2: If you use alcohol, reduce it significantly. It is a central nervous system depressant and worsens perimenopausal mood
bullets.3: Communicate your experience to your partner or family; isolation amplifies mood symptoms

bullets.0: Physical exercise is the single most evidence-based intervention for perimenopausal brain fog
bullets.1: Sleep quality is non-negotiable. Cognitive symptoms worsen sharply and rapidly with poor sleep
bullets.2: Omega-3 supplementation (EPA/DHA 1–2g/day) shows moderate benefit for mood and cognition
bullets.3: Reduce cognitive load: write things down, use structured reminders, give yourself more recovery time

bullets.0: Persistent low mood lasting 2 or more weeks warrants a direct conversation with your GP
bullets.1: Distinguish hormonal mood changes from clinical depression. Both can co-exist and both need treatment
bullets.2: CBT (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy) has strong evidence specifically for perimenopausal anxiety and mood disruption
bullets.3: HRT has documented benefit for mood symptoms linked to oestrogen deficiency. Ask your doctor if this applies to you

B.anuNote: ANU will check in on your mood and anxiety levels every evening. After 14 days, your pattern report will reveal mood cycles, sleep correlations, and your statistically highest-risk days for mood dips. This data makes conversations with your doctor far more productive.

C.label: Physical / GSM Module
C.dominantDomain: Vaginal dryness, painful intercourse, urinary symptoms, joint pain, weight changes, skin and hair
C.trackerFocus: Log physical discomfort levels, urinary frequency, and joint pain. Note week-to-week changes.
C.introTail: Your most significant symptoms are physical, particularly in the genitourinary and musculoskeletal systems. GSM (Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause) is underreported and undertreated. Joint pain, weight changes, and skin and hair changes are also common and often under-acknowledged. All of these are hormone-related and all are addressable.

bullets.0: Non-prescription vaginal moisturisers (non-hormonal): use regularly 2–3 times per week, not only during discomfort
bullets.1: Topical vaginal oestrogen is highly effective, has minimal systemic absorption, and is safe for most women. Ask your doctor
bullets.2: Stay well-hydrated and reduce caffeine and alcohol if you use it, which both worsen urinary urgency and frequency
bullets.3: Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels): 3 sets of 10 daily significantly improve urinary incontinence within 6–8 weeks

bullets.0: Strength training 2–3 times per week is the most effective intervention for joint pain, bone density, and weight stability
bullets.1: Anti-inflammatory diet: reduce refined carbohydrates and added sugars; increase omega-3, leafy greens, and turmeric
bullets.2: Bone health protocol: calcium 1000–1200mg/day through food or supplement + Vitamin D3 1000–2000IU. Discuss dosage with your doctor
bullets.3: Reduce ultra-processed food; perimenopausal metabolic changes mean diet quality matters more than it did in your 30s

bullets.0: Collagen-supporting nutrients: Vitamin C (500mg), zinc, and biotin have evidence for skin and hair quality
bullets.1: Gentle scalp massage and reduced heat styling help slow hair thinning; avoid harsh chemical treatments
bullets.2: Topical retinoids (low-strength) for skin texture and tone. Seek dermatologist guidance before starting
bullets.3: Sun protection is more important than ever; oestrogen loss increases UV sensitivity and skin thinning

C.anuNote: ANU will track your physical symptom patterns across the month. GSM and urinary symptoms often have hormonal timing: they tend to worsen in the days following an oestrogen drop. Your 14-day report will surface this pattern and help your doctor understand the hormonal driver.

D.label: Mixed / Complex Module
D.dominantDomain: Multiple domains at moderate to severe: vasomotor + psychological + physical presenting simultaneously
D.trackerFocus: Track all symptom domains daily. Primary goal: identify which domain is disrupting daily function most.
D.introTail: Your symptom profile spans multiple domains simultaneously. This is more common than most women are told, and it reflects the systemic nature of hormonal change: oestrogen receptors exist throughout the body and brain. A multi-domain profile requires a structured approach: triage, foundation habits, and specialist consultation.

bullets.0: Identify your 2 most disruptive symptoms: not the most frequent, the most disruptive to daily function
bullets.1: Do not attempt to address everything simultaneously; overwhelm worsens outcomes and reduces adherence
bullets.2: Use your ANU daily log for 14 days before making changes. Let the data reveal your highest-impact symptom cluster
bullets.3: Share your full symptom map (not just the most visible symptom) with your doctor at your next visit

bullets.0: Sleep quality is the single lever that affects all symptom domains. Prioritise this above all other interventions
bullets.1: Regular exercise: aerobic + strength combined reduces vasomotor, psychological, and physical symptoms in parallel
bullets.2: Stress reduction: elevated cortisol dysregulates the HPA axis and worsens all three symptom clusters
bullets.3: Nutrition audit: reduce alcohol if you use it, refined sugar, and ultra-processed food. Each worsens symptoms across domains

2.title: Clinical priority for complex symptom profiles

bullets.0: A multi-domain presentation warrants a dedicated menopause specialist consultation, not a general GP visit
bullets.1: Request a comprehensive panel: FSH, LH, oestradiol, thyroid (TSH/FT4), Vitamin D, CBC, fasting lipids
bullets.2: A structured care plan, rather than individual symptom treatments, produces significantly better outcomes
bullets.3: HRT is most impactful for multi-domain perimenopause; discuss risk-benefit with a specialist, not just a general practitioner

D.anuNote: Because your symptoms span multiple domains, ANU will use a daily wellness score rather than single-symptom tracking. After 14 days, your pattern report will rank your symptom domains by daily life impact and suggest a prioritised intervention sequence, so you and your doctor can focus on what matters most first.

GUT.title: Gut Health
GUT.intro: Your responses indicate digestive symptoms that are worth addressing as part of your perimenopause care plan. Gut health is closely connected to hormonal balance. The gut microbiome plays a direct role in oestrogen metabolism through a mechanism called the estrobolome. Changes in perimenopause often disrupt gut flora, worsening digestive symptoms and amplifying hormonal effects.

bullets.0: Declining oestrogen alters gut motility. This is why bloating, constipation, and reflux often worsen in perimenopause
bullets.1: The estrobolome (gut bacteria involved in oestrogen processing) directly influences circulating oestrogen levels
bullets.2: Addressing gut health is not separate from managing perimenopause symptoms. It is part of it
bullets.3: Keep a 7-day food and symptom diary to identify your personal digestive triggers before making changes

bullets.0: Increase dietary fibre gradually to 25–30g per day: wholegrains, legumes, vegetables, and flaxseed
bullets.1: Reduce ultra-processed foods, refined sugars, and artificial sweeteners. All disrupt gut microbiome diversity
bullets.2: If bloating is significant, trial a low-FODMAP approach for 2–4 weeks with guidance from a dietician
bullets.3: Identify and eliminate confirmed intolerances (gluten, dairy, FODMAPs) one at a time, not simultaneously
bullets.4: Stay well-hydrated. 2–2.5 litres of water daily supports bowel regularity and reduces bloating

bullets.0: Probiotic supplementation may support gut health in some women during perimenopause. Discuss suitable options with your dietician.
bullets.1: Prebiotic foods feed beneficial bacteria: garlic, onion, banana, oats, asparagus. Introduce slowly if bloating is present
bullets.2: If antibiotics were taken in the last 12 months, microbiome restoration should be a priority. Discuss with your dietician
bullets.3: Digestive enzymes may support symptoms of bloating and incomplete digestion, particularly useful around meals
bullets.4: Discuss magnesium supplementation with your doctor if constipation is persistent. It supports both gut motility and sleep

GUT.anuNote: ANU will prompt you to log digestive symptoms alongside your main symptom tracking. After 14 days, your pattern report will correlate gut symptoms with your cycle phase, diet entries, and stress levels, revealing whether your gut symptoms are hormonally timed or food-driven. This distinction shapes your treatment direction significantly.

FAMILY.title: Family & Relationship Support
FAMILY.intro: Your responses suggest that perimenopause is affecting your relationships and home environment. This is one of the most underacknowledged dimensions of the transition, and one of the most important. When partners and family members don't understand what is happening, women feel more isolated, symptoms feel more overwhelming, and recovery takes longer. Anuva's family-inclusive model addresses this directly.

0.title: For you: navigating relationships during perimenopause

bullets.0: Name what is happening: telling your partner 'this is a hormonal transition, not a personality change' reframes the dynamic
bullets.1: Choose calm moments (not the middle of a symptom) to have the conversation about what you are experiencing
bullets.2: Be specific about what you need: 'I need you to understand this', 'I need more patience on difficult days', 'I need you to read this guide'
bullets.3: Reduce the invisible load where possible. Perimenopausal fatigue is real and is worsened by carrying everything alone
bullets.4: Give yourself permission to say no to social commitments when symptoms are high. This is not weakness, it is management

1.title: For your partner: what to understand

bullets.0: Perimenopause is a biological transition affecting the brain, body, and nervous system simultaneously. It is not mood or attitude
bullets.1: Irritability, withdrawal, fatigue, and emotional sensitivity are symptoms, not character. They will not last permanently
bullets.2: The most helpful thing a partner can do is listen without trying to fix, and show up with patience rather than solutions
bullets.3: Physical intimacy may change during this time. Vaginal dryness, low libido, and body image changes are real and treatable
bullets.4: Download the Anuva Family Guide for a structured conversation starter you can use together

2.title: For your family: creating a supportive home

bullets.0: Children (especially teenagers) can sense when something has changed. Naming it age-appropriately reduces anxiety for them
bullets.1: Reduce sources of household conflict during high-symptom periods. Communicate needs clearly and early
bullets.2: Enlist family support for practical load (meals, logistics) during difficult weeks. Asking is not a burden, it is communication
bullets.3: Consider an Anuva family session or couples coaching session. Many families find a structured conversation more effective than ad hoc discussion
bullets.4: Community matters: connecting with other women going through the same experience normalises the journey and reduces isolation

FAMILY.anuNote: ANU includes a Family Awareness module that generates a personalised explainer you can share with your partner and family, written for people who are not going through perimenopause themselves. It translates your specific symptom profile into plain language, reducing the gap between what you are experiencing and what your family can understand. Access it from your ANU home screen under 'Share with Family.'

1.label: Early Perimenopause
1.stageContext: Cycles still present. Hormonal fluctuation has begun, so oestrogen levels are starting to shift.
1.menstrualStatus: Periods mostly regular. Cycle may show minor length variation (±3–5 days). Flow changes possible.
1.introLead: You are in the early stage of perimenopause. Your cycles are still present, but hormonal shifts have begun. This is the ideal time to build habits and awareness that will support you through the transition ahead.

medicalFlags.0: Thyroid screening recommended if not done recently
medicalFlags.1: Baseline bone density not yet urgent unless risk factors present
medicalFlags.2: Establish a regular GP check-in cadence

2.label: Mid Perimenopause
2.stageContext: Cycles increasingly irregular. Oestrogen declining more noticeably. Symptom intensity often peaks at this stage.
2.menstrualStatus: Periods irregular: skipping cycles, variable flow, unpredictable timing. Spotting between periods possible.
2.introLead: You are in mid perimenopause, the most hormonally active phase of the transition. Symptoms are often most pronounced at this stage. Your report reflects your current symptom profile and gives you a clear action plan.

medicalFlags.0: Bone density check recommended if not done in last 2 years
medicalFlags.3: Discuss HRT eligibility with your doctor now if symptoms are disruptive

3.label: Late Perimenopause
3.stageContext: Approaching or at 12-month amenorrhoea threshold. Oestrogen at its lowest transitional levels.
3.menstrualStatus: 9–12 months without a period, or approaching this threshold. Any spotting should be discussed with your doctor.
3.introLead: You are in late perimenopause, approaching the menopause threshold. This is a significant milestone in your health journey. Your report focuses on protecting your long-term health while managing current symptoms effectively.

medicalFlags.0: Bone density DXA scan strongly recommended
medicalFlags.3: Review of cancer screening history (breast, cervical, ovarian)
medicalFlags.4: Discuss long-term HRT or alternatives with a specialist
